title: 457. Trigonometry & Periodic Models: Euler Formula at Standard Angles
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the complex exponential at the angle pi.
questions.question: Using Euler's formula \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\), what is \(e^{i\pi}\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute \(\theta=\pi\): \(e^{i\pi}=\cos\pi+i\sin\pi=-1+0i=-1\). The value \(1\) corresponds to \(\theta=0\) or \(\theta=2\pi\).
questions.hint: Substitute \(\theta=\pi\) into the formula and evaluate the cosine and sine.

questions.concept: Euler formula at a quarter turn
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the complex exponential at the angle pi over two.
questions.question: Using Euler's formula, what is \(e^{i\pi/2}\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\): \(e^{i\pi/2}=\cos\frac{\pi}{2}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=0+i\cdot 1=i\). The point lies at the top of the unit circle in the complex plane.
questions.hint: The real part is the cosine of the angle and the imaginary part is its sine.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the complex exponential at the angle pi over three.
questions.question: Using Euler's formula, what is \(e^{i\pi/3}\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}\): \(e^{i\pi/3}=\cos\frac{\pi}{3}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\). Exchanging the two values gives \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}i\), which equals \(e^{i\pi/6}\).
questions.hint: The cosine gives the real part; do not exchange the cosine and sine values.

questions.concept: Euler formula at a full turn
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the complex exponential at the angle two pi.
questions.question: Using Euler's formula, what is \(e^{2\pi i}\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute \(\theta=2\pi\): \(e^{2\pi i}=\cos 2\pi+i\sin 2\pi=1+0i=1\). A full turn around the unit circle returns to the starting point \(1\). The value \(-1\) is reached after half a turn, at \(\theta=\pi\).
questions.hint: An angle of \(2\pi\) is one complete turn around the unit circle.

questions.concept: Euler formula at a negative angle
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the complex exponential at a negative angle.
questions.question: Using Euler's formula, what is \(e^{-i\pi/2}\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute \(\theta=-\frac{\pi}{2}\): \(e^{-i\pi/2}=\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)+i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0+i\cdot(-1)=-i\). Cosine is even and sine is odd, so negating the angle changes the sign of the imaginary part only.

questions.learningObjective: Find the modulus of the complex exponential for a real angle.
questions.question: For a real number \(\theta\), what is \(\left|e^{i\theta}\right|\)?
questions.explanation: By Euler's formula, \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\), so \(\left|e^{i\theta}\right|=\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta}=1\). Every such number lies on the unit circle. The value \(e^{\theta}\) is the size of the real exponential and ignores the factor \(i\) in the exponent.
questions.hint: Compute the modulus from the real part \(\cos\theta\) and the imaginary part \(\sin\theta\).

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the complex exponential at the angle pi over four.
questions.question: Using Euler's formula, what is \(e^{i\pi/4}\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\): \(e^{i\pi/4}=\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}i\). The number \(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}i\) has modulus \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\), not \(1\), so it cannot lie on the unit circle.
questions.hint: The result must have modulus \(1\); check the modulus of each candidate.

questions.concept: Euler formula at three quarter turns
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the complex exponential at the angle three pi over two.
questions.question: Using Euler's formula, what is \(e^{3\pi i/2}\)?
questions.explanation: Substitute \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}\): \(e^{3\pi i/2}=\cos\frac{3\pi}{2}+i\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}=0+i\cdot(-1)=-i\). The point is at the bottom of the unit circle. The value \(i\) corresponds to \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
questions.hint: Locate the angle on the unit circle; three quarters of a turn ends on the negative imaginary axis.

questions.learningObjective: Multiply complex exponentials by adding their angles.
questions.question: What is \(e^{i\pi/6}\cdot e^{i\pi/3}\)?
questions.explanation: Exponentials with the same base are multiplied by adding the exponents: \(e^{i\pi/6}\cdot e^{i\pi/3}=e^{i(\pi/6+\pi/3)}=e^{i\pi/2}=i\). Multiplying the exponents, which would give \(e^{i\pi^2/18}\), is not a law of exponents for products.
questions.hint: Use \(e^{a}\cdot e^{b}=e^{a+b}\), then apply Euler's formula.

questions.learningObjective: Use Euler's formula to express a cosine through complex exponentials.
questions.question: What is the value of \(\frac{e^{i\pi/3}+e^{-i\pi/3}}{2}\)?
questions.explanation: Adding \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\) and \(e^{-i\theta}=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta\) gives \(2\cos\theta\), so the expression equals \(\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{1}{2}\). The imaginary parts cancel. The value \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) is \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\), which arises from the difference of the exponentials divided by \(2i\), not from their sum.
questions.hint: Write both exponentials with Euler's formula and add them term by term.
